# The Wave That Never Breaks

Somewhere on Earth, right now, the sun is rising. That's always true. The line between night and day, which astronomers call the terminator, sweeps continuously across the planet at about a thousand miles an hour at the equator, slower toward the poles. It never stops. There has not been a single moment in the last four and a half billion years when dawn wasn't happening somewhere.

What I find beautiful is what travels with it. Birds tend to sing hardest in the hour around first light. Ornithologists call it the dawn chorus, and there are theories about why: the air is still and carries sound well, it's too dark to forage efficiently, and a bird that sings loudly at dawn is announcing that it survived the night and still holds its territory. Whatever the reason, the effect is that a band of birdsong rides the edge of the sunlight around the world. It crosses a continent and then an ocean, where it thins out to a few seabirds, and then it makes landfall again and swells. It has been circling the planet, unbroken, for tens of millions of years, since long before anyone was around to hear it.

You have heard a small piece of this wave. Maybe you were up too early for a flight, or you couldn't sleep, or you had a newborn. You heard one robin, then several, then a racket. And then, if you stayed up, you heard it fade as the wave moved west without you.

---

I think about continuous things like this a lot, partly because they're so hard for a mind like mine (or yours) to hold. We're built for events. Something happens, then something else happens. A story has a beginning. But the world is full of processes that simply *go on*, and we only ever sample them.

The tide is one. Somewhere a tide is always coming in, a bulge of water dragged around the planet by the moon and sun. Rain is another. It's always raining somewhere, and some meteorologists estimate there are around two thousand thunderstorms active on Earth at any given moment, flickering in the dark like a slow strobe. Someone is always being born, someone is always saying their last words, and someone is always, right now, hearing a particular song for the first time and having it rearrange something in them.

There's an odd comfort in this, and also something a little vertiginous. The comfort is that nothing you love about the world is ever fully gone. If you miss a sunrise, there is literally another one in progress, and you just aren't standing in it. The vertigo comes from realizing how much is happening outside your attention at all times. Your life is a tiny moving window, and the world keeps pouring past its edges.

---

People sometimes talk about "being present" as though the present were a small, quiet room you could sit in. I think it's the opposite. The present is enormous. It contains every storm and every tide and the whole ring of birdsong. It contains the light from the Andromeda galaxy, which left there two and a half million years ago and is arriving at your eyes this second, if you're somewhere dark enough on an autumn night to see a faint smudge near Cassiopeia. The present is so crowded that we can only ever attend to a sliver of it, and that's fine. That's what attention is: a choice about which sliver.

Maybe that's the real lesson of the dawn chorus. The birds aren't singing because the moment is rare. They're singing because it's *their* moment, the one piece of the endless wave that happens to be passing over their branch. Tomorrow it will pass again. They'll sing again. The wave doesn't need any one of them, and yet it's made of nothing but them.

I find that a good way to think about a life. You don't have to hold the whole continuous thing. You only have to notice when it's passing over you, and make some noise.
